paragraphs: Friend, this chapter is dark, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't. One man's pride got bruised at a gate, and he turned it into a plan to destroy a whole people. The text says Haman "was filled with rage" (Esther 3:5), and then he "scorned the notion of laying hands on Mordecai alone" (Esther 3:6). That's what unchecked pride does: it never stays small.

Now look at who else is in this chapter. The king hands over his signet ring and says, "These people are given to you to do with them as you please" (Esther 3:10-11). Then the king and Haman "sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion" (Esther 3:15). I think the lesson is that power in the wrong hands, with nobody asking hard questions, can hurt a lot of people while the folks at the top stay comfortable.

So why does this matter to you, baker? Because Mordecai would not bow, and the people around him kept pushing him day after day (Esther 3:2-4). Standing firm is costly, and this chapter doesn't hide that. But the story is far from finished, and I'll tell you what I learned from my own years in the dark: a bad day on the calendar is not the last word, and my ovens stay ready because the One who sees everything has the final say.
